title: Miami officers gave parents two months, not six: what B1/B2 visas actually allow
excerpt: A family that planned a five-month visit for a grandchild's birth was admitted only until November 2026 at the Miami port of entry — a case immigration attorney Gnanamookan Senthurjothi says exposes the common myth that a B1/B2 visa guarantees a six-month stay.
body:
• A family that planned a five-month US visit was admitted for only two months at the Miami port of entry: return tickets were booked for February 2027, but the I-94 allows a stay only until November 2026.
  • The CBP officer shortened the stay after learning the father still holds a job in India and questioning why the parents needed five months in the US.
  • Immigration attorney Gnanamookan Senthurjothi says a B1/B2 visa does not guarantee admission or a six-month stay: CBP decides the length of stay at entry, and the I-94 date — not the visa — controls when a visitor must leave.
  • Families should verify the I-94 record immediately after entry and treat the date on it as the hard deadline for departure.

Five months planned, two months granted

A family that booked return tickets for February 2027 found its five-month US visit cut to two months at the immigration counter in Miami, The Times of India reported this week. An NRI account posted that the parents had travelled for the birth of their grandchild — but were admitted only until November 2026, meaning they would have to leave before the baby arrives.

The shorter admission came down to one exchange at the counter. The CBP officer noticed that the father still has a job in India and asked why the parents needed a five-month stay, the report said. An analysis by immigration firm EIKOS Global noted that a valid 10-year B1/B2 visa, round-trip tickets and travel insurance did not deliver the six-month stay the family expected — and that officers are tightening scrutiny of long stays, where a five-month leave can raise questions about remote work or overstay risk.

Context: the visa is not the stay

The confusion at the heart of the case is a common one, according to immigration attorney Gnanamookan Senthurjothi, who spoke to The Times of India about the incident. A B1/B2 visa is issued by the US Department of State and lets a traveller present themselves at a US port of entry — it does not guarantee admission. CBP decides whether to admit and for how long, issuing the electronic I-94 arrival/departure record whose date determines the authorized stay.

“CBP officers may consider factors such as the traveller’s stated purpose of visit, previous travel history, frequency and duration of prior stays, and other circumstances presented at the time of admission.”

— Gnanamookan Senthurjothi, immigration attorney

Six-month admissions are common, Senthurjothi said, but not guaranteed. The NRI account had asked whether the parents could stay until their visa expires instead of the November date on the I-94. The attorney’s answer: no — the visa’s expiration date is not the date by which a visitor must leave. The I-94 controls the authorized stay.

Impact: why the officer said no to five months

From the officer’s side, the five-month request had a visible tension: a father with an active job in India seeking nearly half a year away. Officers test whether a visit is genuinely temporary, weighing the requested stay against the traveller’s own circumstances.

VisaVerge’s guidance for Indian parents makes the same point from the preparation side: officers focus on intent — proof of a short visit, funds for the trip, and clear ties to India — while the real length of stay is set by the electronic I-94, not the visa stamp.

“If the purpose of the visit has been completed, leaving the US within the authorized period of admission is generally the safest course from an immigration-compliance perspective.”

— Gnanamookan Senthurjothi, immigration attorney

Diaspora angle: plan around the I-94, not the visa

For NRI families, this case lands close to home. Multi-month parental visits timed to a childbirth are routine in the diaspora, and families often build travel around an expected six-month admission. The Miami case shows that expectation is only a starting point: the officer at the counter can write a shorter date on the I-94, and that date — not the visa’s validity — decides the trip. Parents should arrive ready to explain their plans clearly, with return tickets and evidence of ties back home, and verify the I-94 date on entry.

What’s next for families in this position

Senthurjothi’s five reminders for B1/B2 travellers sum up the lesson: a B1/B2 visa does not guarantee admission; it does not guarantee a six-month I-94; CBP determines the authorized stay at the port of entry; always check the I-94 after entering; and the visa expiration date is not the date by which you must leave. For the Miami family, the question — whether to leave in November as the I-94 requires — is one the visa’s validity cannot answer. Families facing a shortened admission should consult an immigration attorney about their options rather than assume the visa covers them.
